blocks.title: If the station involves counselling or performing an ultrasound examination:

items.text: Wash your hands and introduce yourself.
Confirm the patient's identity.
Explain the purpose of the examination and obtain informed consent.
Ask about the last menstrual period, menstrual pattern, pregnancy possibility, pain, bleeding, discharge and relevant medical history.
Explain the difference between transabdominal and transvaginal ultrasound.
For transvaginal scanning, explain the procedure, obtain specific consent, maintain privacy and use a chaperone according to local policy.
Ensure the patient understands that they can ask questions or stop the procedure at any time.

blocks.text: A transvaginal scan provides detailed images of the pelvic organs. A transabdominal scan may be useful for larger masses or when a transvaginal examination is unsuitable or declined.
Important: If the patient has acute pelvic pain, haemodynamic instability or possible pregnancy complications, urgent clinical assessment takes priority over a routine scan.

subsections.subsection_title: 3. Systematic interpretation of a gynaecological ultrasound

blocks.text: Use the mnemonic U–E–O–A–F–D.
Uterus
Assess size, shape, orientation, contour and myometrium.
Endometrium
Measure thickness where appropriate; assess uniformity, focal lesions and the endometrial cavity.
Ovaries
Assess both ovaries, dimensions, follicles, cysts, solid lesions and blood flow when indicated.
Adnexa
Look for tubal masses, extraovarian lesions and suspicious adnexal abnormalities.
Fluid
Assess for free fluid in the pelvis, including the pouch of Douglas.
Diagnosis and differential
Integrate the ultrasound appearance with age, symptoms, pregnancy status and clinical history.
Also document the scan approach, relevant measurements and technical limitations. Doppler findings can be useful, but normal blood flow does not reliably exclude ovarian torsion.

items.text: Normal-sized uterus for the patient's age and reproductive status.
Smooth external contour.
Myometrium of reasonably uniform echotexture.
No obvious focal mass.
Endometrial cavity without an obvious focal lesion.

blocks.text: Uterine size and endometrial appearance vary with age, parity, hormonal status and menstrual cycle.
The endometrium is assessed in the midline sagittal plane as the maximum double-layer thickness, measured perpendicular to the endometrial cavity.

blocks.title: Its appearance varies during the menstrual cycle:

items.text: Menstrual phase: relatively thin, with variable appearances.
Proliferative phase: progressively thickening endometrium.
Secretory phase: typically thicker and more echogenic.

blocks.text: There is no single normal endometrial thickness threshold for every premenopausal patient. In postmenopausal bleeding, endometrial thickness is interpreted using the relevant guideline and clinical context.
Normal ovaries may contain follicles of different sizes. Their appearance varies with age, menstrual cycle and menopausal status.

items.text: Appropriate ovarian size and morphology.
Follicles without suspicious solid components.
No concerning adnexal mass.
No significant unexplained pelvic free fluid.

blocks.text: A follicle is a normal physiological structure and should not automatically be reported as a pathological cyst.
Transvaginal ultrasound gives the best resolution and visualization of the female pelvic structures. However, it is considered more invasive than the transabdominal approach.

**Machine Positioning**: Position the ultrasound machine on the right side of the patient with the screen facing you. With this configuration you can face both the patient and the ultrasound screen, scanning with your right hand and manipulating buttons on the machine with the other hand. Also position a chair at the foot of the bed to sit in while performing the scan.

When you complete your transvaginal ultrasound exam it is imperative that you disinfect the probe properly using your hospital approved process. You can read the American Institute of Ultrasound in Medicine (AIUM) policy for disinfection [here](https://www.aium.org/officialstatements/57).

content_groups.group_title: Free Fluid Evaluation with Pelvic Ultrasound

blocks.text: Free fluid is one of the most common findings during pelvic ultrasound. A variety of abdominal and pelvic conditions are associated with free fluid accumulation in the pelvis.

In females, free fluid from the abdominal cavity sinks into the pelvic cavity and settles in the **∗Pouch of Douglas**∗ (also called the **Posterior Cul-De-Sac and Rectouterine Pouch**), located posterior to the uterus and anterior to the rectum. Anechoic fluid in this location can be detected by ultrasound imaging using either the transabdominal or transvaginal approaches.
Pouch of Douglas

content_groups.group_title: Normal Amount of Pelvic Free Fluid

blocks.text: Small amounts of free fluid in the pelvis (usually <10 mL but up to ~20 mL near ovulation) can be normal in females (Ritchie, 1986; Hall et al., 1979). This is especially true in patients following ovulation, after menopause, or during early pregnancy. Make sure to look for the free fluid in the **Pouch of Douglas**.
Here are some pelvic ultrasound images of normal amounts of free fluid in the pouch of Douglas.
Small Amount of Free Fluid in Pouch of Douglas; Sagittal Transabdominal Ultrasound
Small Amount of Free Fluid in Pouch of Douglas; Transverse Transabdominal Ultrasound
There are several pathologic conditions (both pelvic and non-pelvic) associated with an abnormal buildup of free fluid in the pelvis.
Here is a list of potential **pelvic causes** of abnormal amounts of free fluid in the Pouch of Douglas:

items.text: Endometriosis
Malignancy
Leiomyoma
Pelvic Inflammatory Disease
Ectopic Pregnancy

blocks.text: Pelvic free fluid accumulation in Pouch of Douglas; Sagittal Transvaginal scan

When you do see a significant amount of free fluid in the Pouch of Douglas make sure to check the right upper quadrant (RUQ) in Morison’s Pouch and the left upper quadrant (LUQ) to evaluate for more free fluid. Remember, free fluid can also be due to non-pelvic causes such as liver cirrhosis (alcohol-related or viral), heart failure, renal failure, and trauma. Uterine abnormalities are a common cause of pelvic complaints that can be detected well using Point-of-Care Ultrasound. You may especially want to assess for uterine pathologies if uterine [measurements](https://www.pocus101.com/ultrasound-machine-basics-knobology-probes-and-modes/) are larger than the normals indicated in the chart below (Nalaboff 2001; Ozcan & DeCherney, 2019).
Normal Uterine Measurements
**Subserosal Fibroids**
**A. Definition**
Uterine fibroids are benign tumours arising from uterine smooth muscle. They may be asymptomatic or cause heavy menstrual bleeding, pelvic pressure, pain, infertility or pregnancy complications.

items.text: Well-defined, round or oval myometrial masses.
Usually hypoechoic or heterogeneous echotexture.
Variable acoustic shadowing.
Distortion of the uterine contour or endometrial cavity, depending on location.
Possible calcification or cystic degeneration.

rows: Projects towards or into the uterine cavity
Particularly associated with heavy bleeding and impaired fertility
May cause bleeding, pain or uterine enlargement
Projects towards the outer uterine surface
May undergo torsion if the stalk twists

content_groups.group_title: D. How to report the image

blocks.text: “The ultrasound demonstrates a well-defined, predominantly hypoechoic mass within the uterine myometrium, measuring approximately 4 cm, consistent with a uterine fibroid. I would document its size, number and location, assess whether it distorts the endometrial cavity, and correlate the findings with the patient's symptoms.”

items.text: Adenomyosis.
Focal adenomyoma.
Endometrial polyp, especially for an intracavitary lesion.
Less commonly, other uterine masses requiring specialist evaluation.
Full blood count and iron studies if heavy menstrual bleeding or anaemia is suspected.
Pregnancy test when relevant.
Transvaginal ultrasound to characterise the fibroids.
Hysteroscopy if an intracavitary lesion requires direct assessment.
MRI if detailed mapping is needed or the diagnosis remains uncertain.

blocks.text: Management depends on symptoms, fibroid location and size, age, fertility goals and patient preference.

items.text: Asymptomatic: observation may be appropriate.
Heavy menstrual bleeding: options may include tranexamic acid, NSAIDs where suitable, hormonal treatment or a levonorgestrel-releasing intrauterine system when appropriate.
Symptomatic fibroids: consider medical treatment, uterine artery embolisation, myomectomy or hysterectomy.
Fertility concerns: assess whether fibroid location and cavity distortion affect reproductive outcomes; discuss fertility-preserving options.

blocks.text: OSCE pearl: A submucosal fibroid is more likely to affect the endometrial cavity than a subserosal fibroid of similar size.
Adenomyosis occurs when endometrial-type tissue is present within the myometrium. It can cause dysmenorrhoea, heavy menstrual bleeding and chronic pelvic pain.

blocks.title: Features that may support adenomyosis include:

items.text: Globular uterine enlargement.
Asymmetrical thickening of the myometrium.
Heterogeneous myometrial echotexture.
Small myometrial cysts.
Echogenic islands or subendometrial lines and buds.
Fan-shaped shadowing.

blocks.text: No single finding is sufficient in every case; the overall pattern and clinical history matter.

“The uterus appears globular, with heterogeneous myometrial echotexture and features suggestive of adenomyosis. I would correlate these findings with the history of dysmenorrhoea and heavy menstrual bleeding. MRI may be considered if ultrasound is inconclusive or further characterisation is needed.”

items.text: Uterine fibroids.
Endometrial pathology causing abnormal bleeding.
Endometriosis, particularly when chronic pelvic pain is present.
NSAIDs where suitable for pain.
Tranexamic acid for heavy menstrual bleeding when appropriate.
Hormonal treatment, including a levonorgestrel-releasing intrauterine system where suitable.
Other progestogen-based or hormonal therapies according to contraindications and patient preference.
Hysterectomy may be considered for severe symptoms when fertility is no longer desired and conservative treatment has failed.

blocks.text: An endometrial polyp is a focal overgrowth of endometrial tissue.

items.text: Focal echogenic lesion within the endometrial cavity.
Smooth or well-defined outline.
Possible single feeding vessel on Doppler.

blocks.text: Symptoms may include intermenstrual bleeding, heavy menstrual bleeding or postmenopausal bleeding, although some polyps are incidental findings.
Investigations: transvaginal ultrasound, saline infusion sonography in selected cases, or hysteroscopy.
Management: observation may be appropriate for selected asymptomatic patients. Hysteroscopic removal and histological assessment may be indicated depending on symptoms and malignancy risk.
A thickened endometrium is a finding, not a diagnosis.

items.text: Normal secretory-phase endometrium.
Endometrial polyp.
Endometrial hyperplasia.
Endometrial carcinoma.
Hormonal medication effects.

blocks.text: Interpret the thickness in relation to menopausal status, cycle timing, bleeding symptoms and risk factors.

In a patient with postmenopausal bleeding, a clearly visualised endometrium measuring 4 mm or less is associated with a low risk of endometrial cancer. Persistent or recurrent bleeding still requires further evaluation, even when the endometrium is thin.

“The endometrium measures ___ mm and appears [uniform/focally thickened/heterogeneous]. The clinical significance depends on the patient's menopausal status, menstrual cycle and symptoms. Given the history of [bleeding or other indication], I would consider further assessment with hysteroscopy or endometrial sampling as appropriate.”
Examiner warning: Do not apply the postmenopausal 4 mm threshold to all premenopausal women.

blocks.text: A haemorrhagic cyst may cause acute pain. Severe pain, haemodynamic instability or suspected rupture requires urgent assessment.

items.text: **Dermoid cyst (mature cystic teratoma)**

blocks.text: Ultrasound Findings of Dermoid Cysts:

Due to the variety of tissue types that make up dermoid cysts, they can have several unique appearances on ultrasound imaging. The presence of two or more of the following findings is suggestive of dermoid cysts:

items.text: Diffuse echogenicity with posterior acoustic enhancement (increased echogenicity posterior to the cyst) – sebaceous tissue and hair; calcified bone or teeth
Echogenic mesh of lines and dots (“dot-dash sign”) due to the presence of hair.
Floating echoic fat globules
Fluid-fluid level – liquids of differing viscosities
Echogenic components.
Acoustic shadowing.
Fat-fluid levels or other characteristic appearances.

blocks.text: Dermoid cysts are usually benign, but complications include torsion. Management depends on symptoms, size, imaging confidence and clinical circumstances.

blocks.text: These features do not independently prove malignancy, but they warrant appropriate specialist risk assessment.

content_groups.group_title: E. How to report an ovarian mass

blocks.text: “The scan demonstrates a [right/left] ovarian lesion measuring ___ cm, with [simple cystic/complex cystic/solid] morphology. I would describe the wall, septations, solid components, papillary projections, Doppler vascularity and presence or absence of ascites. The findings should be correlated with age, menopausal status and symptoms to determine the appropriate risk assessment and follow-up.”

items.text: Pregnancy test when relevant.
Full blood count if bleeding or significant symptoms are present.
CA-125 when indicated by the patient's age, menopausal status and ultrasound risk assessment.
Additional tumour markers for selected masses, particularly in younger patients or when germ-cell tumours are suspected.
MRI for selected indeterminate lesions.
Specialist gynaecological or gynaecological oncology assessment for suspicious masses.

blocks.text: CA-125 is not a stand-alone diagnostic test for ovarian cancer. It can be elevated in benign conditions such as endometriosis and pelvic inflammation.

items.text: Observe selected benign-appearing cysts with appropriate follow-up.
Consider surgery for persistent, symptomatic, enlarging or concerning lesions.
Refer suspicious masses for specialist evaluation and appropriate surgical planning.
Avoid unnecessary surgery when the risk assessment supports conservative management.
Sudden, severe unilateral pelvic pain.
Nausea and vomiting.
Tenderness on abdominal or pelvic examination.
An ovarian cyst or mass may be present.
Enlarged, oedematous ovary.
Follicles displaced towards the periphery.
Abnormal ovarian position.
Free pelvic fluid.

Reduced or absent Doppler flow in some cases.

blocks.text: Critical point: preserved Doppler flow does not exclude ovarian torsion because the ovary has a dual blood supply and torsion may be intermittent or incomplete.

items.text: Arrange urgent gynaecological review.
Assess vital signs and provide appropriate analgesia.
Obtain pregnancy testing and other investigations as clinically indicated.
Do not delay specialist assessment while waiting for definitive imaging if suspicion is high.
Urgent laparoscopy is commonly required for diagnosis and treatment, with detorsion and ovarian preservation whenever feasible.

blocks.text: Model OSCE statement:

“The presentation and ultrasound findings raise concern for ovarian torsion. This is a time-critical surgical emergency. I would arrange immediate gynaecological assessment and would not exclude torsion solely because Doppler flow is present.”
A. Endometrioma
An ovarian endometrioma often has homogeneous low-level, ground-glass internal echoes.
Differential: haemorrhagic cyst and other complex ovarian lesions.
Management: depends on symptoms, fertility plans, lesion features and complications. Specialist assessment is appropriate when imaging is uncertain or concerning.
B. Hydrosalpinx
A dilated, fluid-filled fallopian tube may appear elongated or folded, with characteristic incomplete septations or a waist sign.
Differential: pyosalpinx, tubo-ovarian abscess and other adnexal cystic lesions.
Management: investigate for underlying tubal disease and pelvic infection, assess fertility implications and tailor treatment to the cause.
Ultrasound Findings of Hydrosalpinx:
While fallopian tubes are not normally visible on ultrasound, the dilated uterine tubes of hydrosalpinx can be visualized by the following characteristics on ultrasound imaging:

items.text: Tubular shaped cystic mass discontinuous with the ipsilateral ovary
**Waist sign** – indentations on both sides of the tubular mass
Thin wall
**Beads-on-a-String sign** – cross-sectional view with incomplete septations associated with ∗chronic∗ pelvic inflammation
**Cogwheel sign** – cross-sectional view with thickened longitudinal folds of the uterine tubes associated with ∗acute∗ pelvic inflammation
Tubo-ovarian abscess

blocks.text: Ultrasound Findings of Tubo-ovarian Abscess:
Diagnosis by ultrasound imaging may be difficult due to the varied appearances of tubo-ovarian abscesses. However, some frequently seen ultrasound findings include:

items.text: Adnexal mass: septated, irregular/thick walls, variable internal echogenicity, possible solid areas
Ovary with ill-defined borders (mass obscures both ovary and fallopian tubes)
Hydrosalpinx

blocks.text: May appear as a complex, multilocular adnexal mass with thick walls and internal debris in a patient with pelvic pain and infection.

Management: urgent clinical assessment, pregnancy testing, blood tests and appropriate infection investigations. Broad-spectrum antibiotics are required; drainage or surgery may be necessary depending on severity and response.
A normal ultrasound does not exclude superficial endometriosis or pelvic inflammatory disease. Both diagnoses require clinical correlation.
Polycystic ovarian morphology describes the appearance of the ovaries on ultrasound. It is not synonymous with polycystic ovary syndrome (PCOS).
In adults, PCOS is generally diagnosed using accepted criteria that require two of the following, after excluding relevant alternative causes:

items.text: Clinical or biochemical hyperandrogenism.
Ovulatory dysfunction.
Polycystic ovarian morphology on ultrasound, or an appropriately validated alternative marker in settings where guidelines permit its use.

blocks.text: An ultrasound showing numerous follicles alone does not establish PCOS.
OSCE response:

“The ultrasound may demonstrate polycystic ovarian morphology. I would assess menstrual regularity, clinical features of androgen excess and relevant biochemical findings before determining whether the patient meets diagnostic criteria for PCOS.”
Management is based on the patient's goals and symptoms, including menstrual regulation, metabolic risk reduction, acne or hirsutism treatment, and fertility support when needed.
**Mucinous Cystadenoma**
These types of tumors are the most common type of benign ovarian neoplasm. Patients may appear “gravid” if the mass has grown extensively into the abdomen.
On ultrasound, you can expect to see a cystic mass filled with mucinous material (several small, low-level internal echoes).

blocks.title: Ultrasound findings include a cystic mass with:

items.text: Several thin septations that undulate with transducer palpation.
Few/no internal echoes

blocks.title: These tumors are malignant and appear on ultrasound as cystic masses with:

items.text: Thick septa
Mural nodularity
Solid tissue with internal vascularization
Another clue pointing toward malignancy is the presence of ascites, which is generally absent in benign conditions

blocks.text: Q1. What are the typical ultrasound features of uterine fibroids?
Well-defined myometrial masses, often hypoechoic or heterogeneous, sometimes with acoustic shadowing or calcification. Their location and relationship to the endometrial cavity are important.
Q2. How can adenomyosis be distinguished from fibroids?
Adenomyosis more often causes a globular uterus, heterogeneous myometrium, asymmetrical thickening and myometrial cysts. Fibroids are more often discrete, well-defined masses. Overlap occurs.
Q3. Does a thickened endometrium always mean endometrial cancer?
No. Thickness varies with the menstrual cycle and may reflect benign polyps, hyperplasia or other causes. Interpretation depends on menopausal status, symptoms and risk factors.
Q4. What ultrasound features are concerning in an ovarian mass?
Solid components, papillary projections, irregular walls or septations, ascites and other evidence of extraovarian disease warrant further risk assessment.
Q5. Can normal Doppler flow exclude ovarian torsion?
No. Preserved flow does not exclude torsion. Clinical suspicion requires urgent gynaecological assessment.
Q6. What is the difference between a hydrosalpinx and a tubo-ovarian abscess?
A hydrosalpinx is a fluid-distended fallopian tube. A tubo-ovarian abscess is a complex inflammatory collection involving the tube and ovary, usually associated with infection.
Q7. Does polycystic ovarian morphology establish PCOS?
No. PCOS requires the appropriate combination of diagnostic features and exclusion of alternative causes.
Q8. When should an ovarian mass be referred urgently?
When there are suspicious malignant features, acute severe pain suggesting torsion or rupture, significant bleeding, or other signs of clinical deterioration.

items.text: Reporting an ovarian cyst without describing its morphology, size and location.
Confusing adenomyosis with a discrete fibroid.
Diagnosing PCOS from ultrasound alone.
Using the same endometrial thickness threshold for premenopausal and postmenopausal patients.
Assuming that normal Doppler flow excludes ovarian torsion.
Treating CA-125 as proof of ovarian cancer.
Reassuring a patient with a suspicious adnexal mass without appropriate risk assessment.
Forgetting pregnancy testing in a reproductive-age patient with pelvic pain.
Failing to escalate acute pelvic pain, suspected torsion or a possible tubo-ovarian abscess.
